messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Adding a silence to sound alters measures of sound dissimilarity
messages.body_plain:
Le 20/03/2015 16:47, Jorge Velásquez a écrit :

> Hi there,
>
> I'm trying to understand if having silence in recordings could alter the dissimilarity indices computed on them (eg. diffwave, ks.dist etc). I'll explain myself in code:
>
> #For the recording tico, I'm going to add a silence at the end and middle of it. Then I'll compute the ks.dist, which if my understanding of the index is correct should remain unaffected as it compares two frequency spectra.
>
> data(tico)
> tico1<-addsilw(tico,at="end",d=10,output="Wave")
> tico2<-addsilw(tico,at="middle",d=10,output="Wave")
> ks.dist(spec(tico1), spec(tico2),plot=T)
>
> Which returns a distance of 0.1437989. Samething happens with other distance measures (kl.dist, diffwave, diffcumspefc). So clearly I am misunderstanding something. Can someone explain?
>
> Best,
>
> Jorge
>
>

> --
> You received this message because you are subscribed to the Google Groups "seewave" group.
> To unsubscribe from this group and stop receiving emails from it, send an email to seewave+u...@googlegroups.com.
> For more options, visit https://groups.google.com/d/optout.
Dear Jorge,
Yes ks.dist() returns a value != 0 because the two spectra of the complete inout are indeed quite different :
par(mfrow=c(2,1))
spec(tico1)
spec(tico2)

but this difference will tend to 0 if you use mean spectra instead:

par(mfrow=c(3,1))
meanspec(tico1)
meanspec(tico2)
ks.dist(meanspec(tico1, plot=FALSE), meanspec(tico2, plot=FALSE), plot=TRUE)

Jerome

messages.subject: Re: Acoustic Entropy Index vs. Acoustic Diversity Index
messages.subject_clean: Acoustic Entropy Index vs. Acoustic Diversity Index
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I actually understand the confusion between all these indices.

The index H was first introduced by Sueur et al (2008). It is made of two sub-indices, namely Ht and Hf. Ht computes the Shannon evenness of the temporal signal (on the Hilbert amplitude envelope) and Hf computes the Shannon evenness of the mean spectrum obtained after computing a STFT (ie a spectrogram).

Later Pijanowki et al (2011), Villanueva-Rivera et al (2011), Pekin et al (2012) derived an index named H' or ADI based on Hf. If I am not mistaken (Luis might confirm) this index mainly differs in that it is not scaled between 0 and 1 as Hf is (Shannon diversity versus Shannon evenness), in the control of the frequency binning obtained with the STFT and also in the use of an amplitude threshold as detailed here <http://www.cran.r-project.org/web/packages/soundecology/vignettes/intro.html> and there <http://www.cran.r-project.org/web/packages/soundecology/vignettes/changeADI.html>.

Jerome

Le lundi 9 mars 2015 02:27:43 UTC+1, Danny Zurc a écrit :
> Hello.
>
> My name is Danny Zurc, and I’m doing my master’s thesis on bioacoustics of Colombian bats. I come from a systematics background so I am new to seewave and R in general. I’m interested in computing bioacoustics diversity indices on my sound files. However I am confused on how exactly are the Total Entropy calculated by seewave (function H) and the Acoustic Diversity Index (function acoustic_diversity) different. From what I gather, they’re both based on Shannon’s entropy but they’re clearly giving me very different values. Could someone here explain?
>
> Thank you so much.
>

messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Re: Acoustic Entropy Index vs. Acoustic Diversity Index
messages.body_plain:
Danny and list,

First, to clarify. The ADI was not based on Hf.

Second, the main difference is that H is measuring entropy in both time and frequency space, while ADI is measuring it in frequency space only. We were analyzing insanely long files (~15 min), and we noticed that the variation in time was very small, most of the differences between sites and time of the day were in the frequencies occupied. So, we ended up making bins of 1000Hz and counting everything above a threshold, to avoid counting the faint sounds and noise.

I hope this helps. Feel free to contact me if you need more info.

Luis J. Villanueva
http://research.CoquiPR.com

messages.subject: Fundamental Frequency Detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to identify the fundamental frequency of a toad call. However, I am a little confused about what the best function for the job would be - ceps() or fund()? Also on a more theoretical note, is the fundamental frequency usually expected to be the same as the dominant?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Fundamental Frequency Detection
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The function ceps() computes the cepstrum which can be used to identify the fundamental frequency (lowest or first "peak" of the cepstrum).
The function fund() uses ceps() to track the fundamental frequency at a specific location or along the signal with a sliding window. This is a short-term function as the stFt.
fund() is the function to use if you want to get direct results. You can consider that fund() is equivalent to dfreq() and ceps() to spec() for a Cesptrum / Fourier transform.

The fundamental and dominant frequencies can be different due to the action of resonators.

Best

Jerome

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jerome,

I tried the fund() function and had a follow up question :

These are the details of my function - fund(s1, f=44100,wl = 512, ovlp = 95, fmax=900, type="l",threshold=NULL,plot=TRUE)

This gives me a graph of frequency plotted against time (attached with this email). However there are several peaks in this diagram and I am unsure of how to extract information on fundamental frequency from it.

Also, what information do you use to decide the value to be set for fmax?

Sorry if I am missing something, I am relatively new to acoustic analysis.

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Fundamental Frequency Detection
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

This is the result of the fundamental frequency tracking against time. There is no peak to look for in this graph.

The line you draw is somohow artifial, you should use type="p", this will depict the fundamental frequency detected per sliding window.

I think you should go through a bit of theory before. You may like to go through Hopp et al Animal acoustic communication, Springer.

Best

Jerome
